title: Facing the London: Black's counter-pyramid and the moves that bite

difficulty.label: Black player tired of losing slowly to the London

objective.summary: Your opponent chose the London: a system they play every game and you face twice a season. Challenge it in the order that asks real questions — ...c5 immediately, the counter-pyramid, ...Bd6 against their prized bishop — and know where their plan is headed (Ne5, Bd3, the h-file) before it gets there.

planClasses.label: Trade or chase the f4 bishop (...Bd6, ...Nh5)
planClasses.description: The London is named after one bishop: every tempo it spends staying alive (Bg3, h3) is a tempo their attack never gets. ...Bd6 is the structural challenge; ...Nh5 is the concrete one — the spine plays the first and classifies the second.

planClasses.label: Hit b2 while the bishop is away (...Qb6)
planClasses.description: Position-specific: the bishop's departure from c1 leaves b2 with no defender at all (machine-counted 2026-08-15: one White piece bears on b2 while the bishop is home, that piece being the bishop; zero once it is on f4), and after e3 the ...Qb6 jab arrives before c3/Nbd2 coordination is complete. Its catalogued form is the Poisoned Pawn row this pack's deviation transposes into, move for move.

planClasses.label: Solve the c8 bishop (...b6/...Bb7)
planClasses.description: The counter-pyramid's honest cost is the c8 bishop behind ...e6. The plan that pays it off: ...b6, ...Bb7, and central breaks timed for when the long diagonal opens — the same asymmetry the London player is counting on, worked from the other side.

annotations: Challenge immediately, before the pyramid is finished. At your band most players drift with ...e6 first (28.1%); the immediate ...c5 (11.7%) is the catalogued mainline row and the move that makes White's construction order matter.
The moment the c1 bishop can never come home. Your sharpest sidestep lives here — ...Qb6, classified below — and the spine's slower road keeps the tension instead.
Develop toward the tension: the knight leans on d4 and keeps ...cxd4 a live threat that White must always price in.
The counter-pyramid, with its cost stated honestly: your c8 bishop is now the worst piece on the board, and the third plan class exists to fix that.
Their wall is complete; yours is one move behind. This is YOUR decision point: the ...Bd6 challenge, the ...cxd4 release, or queenside plans first — the drill is choosing on purpose.

Ask the system question: trade the London bishop or make it move again. Either answer costs White something — the trade costs the attack's engine, Bg3 costs a tempo and parks the bishop where ...Bxg3 opens White's h-file, not yours.
The usual answer. Note what it tells you: White will recapture hxg3 if you ever trade, and wants Bd3/Ne5/f4 next. Your remaining spine moves are played knowing that plan.
Castle into the plan you can name: Bd3 aims at h7, Ne5 wants f4 behind it. Naming it is most of surviving it — the checkpoint asks you to.
The third plan begins: ...Bb7 next, and the c8 bishop stops being the position's apology. Played now because White's slow build granted the tempo.

The London's signature arrives — with its arithmetic: if ...Nxe5 dxe5, the pawn forks d6 and f6 (machine-walked geometry), so the knight is usually tolerated, undermined with ...f6 ideas, or answered by completing ...Bb7 first. Past the book from here: play the middlegame you just watched White build.

checkpoints.label: 6.c3 — challenge, release, or queenside: choose your handling
Castled — name White's plan before it happens
Ne5 arrives — you knew it was coming
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 4...Qb6 — the position after it is FEN-identical to the London System: Poisoned Pawn Variation row (reached there by 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 order; transposition machine-verified this session). The queen hits the b2 square the bishop left behind; White's catalogued answer is 5.Nc3. The sharpest anti-London try at this band, and a different pack's full subject.

6...cxd4 releases the tension; the walked recapture is 7.exd4, keeping White's c3-d4 chain and opening the e-file side of their pyramid. Releasing costs you the standing ...cxd4 threat — after it, White's pieces stop having to price it in. Sound, and slightly obliging.

7...Nh5 hunts the bishop a second time. Two tempi for the bishop pair is the open question the classification refuses to answer for you: the walked line confirms only that the knight stands safe on h5 and the bishop must decide again.

7...Bxg3 8.hxg3 resolves the bishop question by handing White the half-open h-file toward your castled king — derived from the walked recapture, and exactly why the spine waits: taking on g3 is soundest before ...O-O, or when the h-file cannot matter.

feedbackClaims.text: At the 1400/1600/1800 rating bands (Lichess blitz+rapid, 2024-01 through 2026-07), the London position after 3.Bf4 was reached 3,851,145 times and Black scores 44.5% against White's 50.4% — among the family roots measured in this repo's priority artifact, this is one of the worst results for the receiving side. This pack exists to move that number.
Your peers' current habit is 3...e6 (28.1% of games); the immediate 3...c5 this pack drills is chosen only 11.7% of the time — the catalogued mainline is, at your band, the road not taken.

The London player plays this structure every White game; you face it occasionally. Drilling the first eight defensive moves until they are automatic is worth more here than in any opening you chose yourself — the preparation asymmetry is the whole reason anti-opening packs exist.

The ...Qb6 deviation's identity is the London System: Poisoned Pawn Variation row of the same file: its position after 4...Qb6 (via 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5) and this pack's (via 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6) were verified FEN-identical with a chessops scratch harness this session.
